clue.text: Call that is unsuitably tricky

definitions.text: Call that is unsuitably tricky

parts.note: in bridge a call is a bid; a no-trump contract has no trump suit, so it is 'unsuitable', and it promises to take nine tricks, so it is 'tricky'

explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, a bid of three in no trumps contracts to win nine of the thirteen tricks with no suit ranking as trumps.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a bridge bid made without any trump suit, aiming to take nine tricks: an unsuited, trick-taking call.

clue.text: And nothing can be found in the shack

definitions.text: And nothing can be found in the shack

indicators.note: says the words before it are located inside the hut

parts.note: a hut is a shack
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A bare cabin with nothing at all inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue pictures a poor man's shack, where charity is all that turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift of food or money to the needy is what the poor occupant of an empty shack depends on.

clue.text: Always to the poet that is quite. uncanny

definitions.text: uncanny

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: A verse lover declares that it is always quite uncanny.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something strange and frightening, beyond natural explanation; they are synonyms.

clue.text: "Haste thee —, and bring with thee Jest and youthful jollity" (Milton)

definitions.text: "Haste thee —, and bring with thee Jest and youthful jollity" (Milton)

parts.words: "Haste thee —, and bring with thee Jest and youthful jollity" (Milton)
parts.note: the opening of the summons in Milton's L'Allegro, with the word addressed left blank

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Milton's L'Allegro calls on a mythical spirit, 'Haste thee ..., and bring with thee / Jest and youthful Jollity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's poem addresses a female nature spirit of classical myth, and that word fills the dash.

clue.text: Henry VII got up emblematically

definitions.text: Henry VII got up emblematically

parts.note: Henry VII was the first Tudor king
rose means got up

explanation.surface: The first Tudor king climbed to his feet in a symbolic way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emblematically' turns the plain charade into the emblem: Henry VII is TUDOR and 'got up' is ROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry VII combined the red and white roses of Lancaster and York into the dynasty's heraldic badge.

clue.text: A sort of overall fellow ?

definitions.text: A sort of overall fellow ?

parts.note: an ulster is a long loose overcoat, an outer garment worn over all
a man is a fellow

explanation.surface: Someone who is a thorough, all-round sort of chap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overall' looks like 'general', but it is a garment: an ulster coat. The whole is a native of Ulster, Northern Ireland's province.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Irish province shares his name with a heavy overcoat, so he is jokingly an 'overall fellow'.

clue.text: He seems a cold hearted professional

definitions.text: He seems a cold hearted professional

indicators.note: having something as its heart, so the cold word sits in the middle of the professional

parts.note: pro is short for professional
rime is frost, the cold white coating on plants

explanation.surface: A man who looks like an unfeeling career type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He seems' because the answer looks like a Spanish man's name but is the old card game Primero; RIME goes into PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: This Tudor gambling card game has a name that reads like a Spanish man's, so it only 'seems' to be a he.

clue.text: How. hands work with a twelve-hour day

definitions.text: How. hands work with a twelve-hour day

parts.words: How. hands work with a twelve-hour day
parts.note: workers on a twelve-hour shift labour long, and a clock's hands circle its face

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' means workers as well as a clock's pointers, which go once round in twelve hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Working all day and night without stopping is the idiom; literally, it is the full circuit a clock's hands make.

clue.text: Fate of many a team in an English summer

definitions.text: Fate of many a team in an English summer

parts.words: Fate of many a team in an English summer
parts.note: rain stops play so often in England that sides are 'beaten' by the climate rather than the opposition

explanation.walkthrough: A cricket joke: in a wet English summer many matches are lost or abandoned to rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The word normally means worn by exposure to wind and rain; here it is read as defeated by the climate.

clue.text: The man in possession

definitions.text: The man in possession

parts.note: read plainly, the person who possesses something, though the phrase also suggests a bailiff put in to occupy a house

explanation.walkthrough: A 'man in possession' was the bailiff's man left in a debtor's house; the answer is the plainer reading, the one who possesses.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever has possession of property holds title to it, which is exactly what a proprietor or holder is.

clue.text: Purchased by R. L. S. from Father Adam

definitions.text: Purchased by R. L. S. from Father Adam

parts.words: Purchased by R. L. S. from Father Adam
parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson bought his donkey from a dealer called Father Adam, as told in Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes

explanation.walkthrough: R. L. S. is Robert Louis Stevenson; in Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes he buys the donkey he names Modestine from Father Adam for sixty-five francs and a glass of brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of the she-donkey Stevenson bought and walked across the Cévennes, so the clue points to her by the purchase.

clue.text: She was " all tears "

definitions.text: She was " all tears "

parts.note: Hamlet says his mother followed his father's body 'like ..., all tears'

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Hamlet: Gertrude went to the funeral 'like Niobe, all tears'. In Greek myth Niobe wept endlessly for her slain children and was turned to a weeping rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Niobe is the mythological mother whose grief for her lost children made her the type of endless weeping.

clue.text: The object of Haggard's novel

definitions.text: The object of Haggard's novel

parts.note: Rider Haggard wrote the novel She; the objective case of that pronoun is wanted

explanation.surface: A literary question: what was Rider Haggard's adventure novel really about?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like 'aim or subject matter', but it is grammar: Haggard's novel is She, and the object form of 'she' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the pronoun she becomes this form when it is the object of a verb, as in 'I saw ...'.

clue.text: Partly preselective, according: to choice

definitions.text: according: to choice

indicators.note: only a part of the word preselective is used, so the letters sit inside it

explanation.surface: Something partly preselected, made according to choice.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective this means chosen or picked out, so something done by choice fits.

clue.text: His arch is featured in Rome

definitions.text: His arch is featured in Rome

parts.words: His arch is featured in Rome
parts.note: the Arch of ... stands at the end of the Forum in Rome, celebrating that emperor's capture of Jerusalem

explanation.walkthrough: The Arch of Titus, built after the emperor's death, stands on the Via Sacra in the Roman Forum.
explanation.definitionFit: This Roman emperor is commemorated by the triumphal arch in the Forum, so the arch identifies him.

clue.text: The price of courtship ?

definitions.text: The price of courtship ?

parts.note: spooning was old slang for courting, and a bill is the price charged

explanation.walkthrough: To 'spoon' was to court or canoodle, and a bill is what you pay: the result is a wading bird with a spoon-shaped beak.
explanation.definitionFit: The wading bird with the flat, spatulate beak has a name that splits into old slang for courting plus a charge.

clue.text: Notice of performance of The Tempest ?

definitions.text: Notice of performance of The Tempest ?

parts.words: Notice of performance of The Tempest ?
parts.note: a notice of a show of Shakespeare's play, read as a warning that a real tempest is coming

explanation.surface: A theatre bill announcing a staging of Shakespeare's The Tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: A storm cone was the canvas cone hoisted at British coastguard stations to warn shipping of a gale.
explanation.definitionFit: The hoisted cone was the official signal that a gale was expected, a notice that a tempest would 'perform'.

clue.text: Does he procure the fur of the stone marten, for instance?

definitions.text: Does he procure the fur of the stone marten, for instance?

parts.words: Does he procure the fur of the stone marten, for instance?
parts.note: the saying 'he would skin a flint' describes a miser; here stone is taken as flint

explanation.walkthrough: A miser is said to be so mean he would skin a flint (a stone). The stone marten is a real animal, used to make the stone furry.
explanation.definitionFit: A mean person is said to be stingy enough to strip the skin from a stone, and the name comes from that saying.

clue.text: One is come to cut down expenses

definitions.text: cut down expenses

indicators.note: an old-style faint signal: the phrase before it is brought round to a new order of its letters

explanation.surface: Someone has arrived to trim the household budget.
explanation.walkthrough: A 1950s clue with almost no anagram signal: 'to' links 'One is come' to its rearrangement, and the nine letters are simply reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To spend less and avoid waste is to reduce one's outgoings, the plain sense of cutting down expenses.

clue.text: Reverse of a throw in

definitions.text: Reverse of a throw in

parts.note: turn 'in' and 'throw' around, giving out and a word for throw, and the order switches

explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw-in' suggests football, but read 'in-throw' as its opposite: out for in, cast for throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone rejected by society has been thrown out, the opposite of being brought into the fold.

clue.text: A man of wealth cut off without even a shilling in Scotland

definitions.text: A man of wealth

parts.note: in Scotland 'na' means not or no, so a man cut off without even a shilling is left 'na bob'
a bob was British slang for a shilling, the old coin worth twelve pence

explanation.surface: A rich man disinherited and left penniless north of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Scotland' signals the Scots word NA (not). A bob was the old British shilling coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally a governor in Mughal India, the title came to mean any very rich man, especially one back from India.

clue.text: Letters delivered with the early tea :?

definitions.text: Letters delivered with the early tea :?

parts.words: Letters delivered with the early tea :?
parts.note: in a grand house the morning post came up on the tray with the tea, so it arrived at the sleeper's side

explanation.walkthrough: In a well-run household the servant brought letters along with early morning tea, so this is post taken to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The upright at each corner of a bedstead splits into the place the mail reaches and the mail itself.

clue.text: Shakespeare's. was small, according to Jonson

definitions.text: Shakespeare's. was small, according to Jonson

parts.words: Shakespeare's. was small, according to Jonson
parts.note: Ben Jonson wrote that Shakespeare had 'small ... and less Greek'

explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's memorial poem says Shakespeare had 'small Latin and less Greek'.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of ancient Rome is the one Jonson said Shakespeare knew only a little of.

clue.text: Any story-teller can achieve this

definitions.text: Any story-teller can achieve this

parts.note: a story-teller is also a childish word for a liar, and anyone can tell a small lie

explanation.walkthrough: 'Story-teller' suggests an author, but in nursery language telling stories means telling lies.
explanation.definitionFit: A trivial untruth is what a 'story-teller' in the nursery sense tells, and it takes no talent.

clue.text: Rachael's father is become so vulgar

definitions.text: vulgar

indicators.note: the father's name has changed into something new, so his letters are rearranged

parts.note: in Genesis Laban is the father of Rachel, Jacob's wife

explanation.surface: A biblical patriarch has turned coarse.
explanation.walkthrough: Laban, Rachel's father in Genesis, 'is become' (archaic for has become) the answer by rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Here vulgar has its older sense of commonplace or trite, which is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Decapitation was doubly ineffective to deal with this

definitions.text: Decapitation was doubly ineffective to deal with this

parts.words: Decapitation was doubly ineffective to deal with this
parts.note: the many-headed serpent of Lerna grew two heads for every one Hercules cut off

explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth, each head Hercules struck from the Lernaean monster was replaced by two, so cutting heads off made matters doubly worse.
explanation.definitionFit: The monster of Hercules' second labour regrew two heads for each one lopped off, so beheading it backfired twice over.

clue.text: Young people are often thrilled at its, loss

definitions.text: Young people are often thrilled at its, loss

parts.words: Young people are often thrilled at its, loss
parts.note: to lose your ... is to fall in love, which delights the young

explanation.walkthrough: Losing something is normally bad, but 'losing your heart' means falling in love.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ stands for one's affections; giving it away to someone is the idiom for falling in love.

clue.text: Sort of government England does not love, according to Disraeli

definitions.text: Sort of government England does not love, according to Disraeli

parts.words: Sort of government England does not love, according to Disraeli
parts.note: Disraeli declared in 1852 that 'England does not love ...'

explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli's line in the Commons, 'England does not love coalitions', is quoted almost word for word.
explanation.definitionFit: A government formed by several parties sharing power is the kind Disraeli said the English distrust.

clue.text: In Beer you must get on by yourself

definitions.text: by yourself

indicators.note: placed first, In says the next piece is to be put inside the drink

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Drinking advice: in the pub you have to make your own way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' opens the clue but governs the next two pieces; 'you must get' merely links them.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with no one else, unaccompanied, is the sense of the phrase 'by yourself'.

clue.text: A little "bird told me-was this the one ?

definitions.text: A little "bird told me-was this the one ?

parts.words: A little "bird told me-was this the one ?
parts.note: the saying 'a little bird told me' hides who gossiped; the playground name for a sneak is a kind of bird

explanation.walkthrough: The tit is a small bird, and 'tell-tale tit' is the British playground taunt for a child who sneaks to grown-ups.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's sneak is called a little bird that tells tales, so it is the 'little bird' of the saying.
